items.prompt: What is the hard outer covering of a turtle or tortoise called?

options.label: The shell
options.feedback: Correct. The shell is the turtle's protective outer covering, made of bone and keratin.

options.label: The carapace
options.feedback: The carapace is only the top part of the shell, not the whole covering. The shell also includes the bottom part, called the plastron.

options.label: The plastron
options.feedback: The plastron is only the bottom part of the shell, not the entire covering. The full shell includes both the plastron and the carapace.

options.label: The scute
options.feedback: A scute is a single plate on the shell's surface, not the whole covering. The shell is made of many scutes attached to bone underneath.

items.ok_line: The shell is the turtle's protective outer covering.
items.ko_line: Each of those names refers to only a part of the shell.
items.exp_text: The shell is the entire hard covering, made of bone covered by keratin plates called scutes. It has a top part (carapace) and a bottom part (plastron). This is what protects the turtle's body.

items.prompt: Which part of the turtle's body is permanently attached to its shell?

options.label: Its tail
options.feedback: The tail is outside the shell and can be tucked in, but it is not fused to the shell. Only the ribs and spine are attached directly.

options.label: Its head
options.feedback: The head is not attached to the shell; it can pull in and out. The shell is fused to the bird's ribs and spine.

options.label: Its ribs and spine
options.feedback: Correct. The shell is actually part of the skeleton—the ribs and spine are fused to it, so the turtle cannot crawl out of its shell.

options.label: Its legs
options.feedback: Legs are outside the shell and can retract, but they are not fused to it. Only the ribs and spine are built into the shell.

items.ok_line: The ribs and spine are part of the shell.
items.ko_line: Only the ribs and spine are fused to the shell.
items.exp_text: The turtle's ribs and spine grow into the shell, making it part of the animal's own skeleton. That is why a turtle can never leave its shell; the shell is its body.

items.prompt: What does the turtle's shell feel when you scratch it?

options.label: Nothing, because it is dead material
options.feedback: The outer layer is dead keratin, but underneath the shell has living bone and nerves, so the turtle can feel touch on it.

options.label: The touch, because the shell has nerves
options.feedback: Correct. The shell is living bone covered by keratin, and it contains nerves, so a turtle feels a scratch on its shell.

options.label: Only pressure, not light touch
options.feedback: Turtles can feel light touches on their shell, not just heavy pressure, because the shell has sensory nerves throughout the bone.

options.label: The scratch as pain, because the shell is delicate
options.feedback: A normal scratch is not painful, but the shell can feel it. Pain would occur only if the shell is damaged deeply enough to injure the living tissue.

items.ok_line: Nerves in the shell sense touch.
items.ko_line: The shell is living tissue with nerves.
items.exp_text: The turtle's shell is not a lifeless armor; it is living bone with blood vessels and nerves. That is why a turtle flinches when you scratch its shell—it feels the touch.

items.prompt: How does a turtle breathe, given that its ribs are fused into its shell?

options.label: It cannot breathe at all when inside its shell
options.feedback: That is not true; turtles breathe fine inside their shells. They use muscles that move other parts of the body to change air pressure in the lungs.

options.label: It breathes through its skin like a frog
options.feedback: Turtles have lungs, not skin breathing. They inhale air through their nostrils and into their lungs, just at a different mechanism because the ribs are fixed.

options.label: It uses its throat to pump air in and out
options.feedback: Throat movements help in some turtles, but the main breathing uses muscles attached to the inside of the shell and the organs to expand the lungs. There is no diaphragm like ours.

options.label: It uses special muscles that move the organs and shell to change lung volume
options.feedback: Correct. Turtles have muscles attached to the shell and internal organs that squeeze the lungs to push air out, and relax to let air in, so they can breathe without moving ribs.

items.ok_line: Turtles use special muscles to breathe.
items.ko_line: Turtles have a different way to inflate lungs.
items.exp_text: Since the ribs are part of the shell and cannot move, turtles use muscles that attach to the shell and to the organs. Contracting these muscles changes the volume of the lungs, pulling air in and pushing it out.

items.prompt: What is the name of the lower part of a turtle's shell?

options.label: Plastron
options.feedback: Correct. The plastron is the bottom (belly) side of the shell, while the top is called the carapace.

options.label: Carapace
options.feedback: The carapace is the upper (back) part, not the lower part. The lower part is the plastron.

options.label: Scute
options.feedback: A scute is one of the individual keratin plates covering the shell, not the bottom section. The bottom section is the plastron.

options.label: Bridge
options.feedback: The bridge is the side area connecting the top and bottom parts, not the entire lower part. The lower part is the plastron.

items.ok_line: The lower shell is the plastron.
items.ko_line: Carapace, scute, and bridge each mean a different part.
items.exp_text: The turtle's shell has two main sections: the carapace on top and the plastron underneath. The plastron is the flat, bottom part that protects the belly.

items.prompt: What do the scutes on a turtle's shell consist of?

options.label: Bone
options.feedback: Bone is underneath the scutes, but the scutes themselves are made of a different material. The scutes are the outer plates.

options.label: Cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage is not what forms the outer plates. The shell's outer layer is made of keratin, like your fingernails.

options.label: Keratin
options.feedback: Correct. Scutes are made of keratin, the same tough protein that makes up your fingernails and hair, which covers the bone of the shell.

options.label: Chitin
options.feedback: Chitin is the material in insect exoskeletons, not in turtle shells. Turtle scutes are made of keratin.

items.ko_line: The outer plates are keratin, not bone or chitin.
items.exp_text: The scutes are the hard, slightly rough plates on the outside of the shell. They are made of keratin, which is the same protein that forms your fingernails, giving them strength and some flexibility.

items.prompt: Which type of turtle has webbed feet with claws for swimming?

options.label: Tortoise
options.feedback: Tortoises live on land and have round, stumpy feet without webbing. They are not swimmers.

options.label: Aquatic turtle
options.feedback: Correct. Aquatic turtles, like pond turtles and sea turtles, have webbed feet or flippers to push through water, with claws for gripping surfaces.

options.label: Box turtle
options.feedback: Box turtles are land-dwelling but have moderately webbed feet; they are not fully aquatic and their feet are not primarily for swimming. This description fits aquatic turtles better.

options.label: Snapping turtle
options.feedback: Snapping turtles are aquatic and have webbed feet, but the key distinction here is between tortoises and aquatic turtles. Aquatic turtle is the broader correct group.

items.ok_line: Webbed feet help aquatic turtles swim.
items.ko_line: Tortoises have stumpy feet, not webbed ones.
items.exp_text: Aquatic turtles have webbing between their toes and claws to paddle through water and climb onto logs. Tortoises, which live on land, have round, stumpy feet built for walking on dirt and rock.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between a turtle and a tortoise?

options.label: Turtles have shells, tortoises do not
options.feedback: Both turtles and tortoises have shells. The difference is in their habitat and body shape, not the presence of a shell.

options.label: Tortoises can swim, turtles cannot
options.feedback: It is the opposite: tortoises live on land and are poor swimmers, while many turtles live in water and swim well.

options.label: Turtles are land animals, tortoises are water animals
options.feedback: That is reversed. Tortoises are land animals, while turtles (in common usage) are often aquatic or semi-aquatic.

options.label: Tortoises live on land, turtles live in or near water
options.feedback: Correct. Tortoises are strictly land-dwelling with stumpy feet, while turtles generally live in water (fresh or sea) and have webbed feet or flippers.

items.ok_line: Tortoises are land-dwellers; turtles live in water.
items.ko_line: Both have shells; the key is where they live.
items.exp_text: The main distinction is habitat: tortoises are land animals that cannot swim well and have heavy, domed shells and stubby feet. Turtles live in water most of their lives and have lighter, flatter shells and webbed feet or flippers.

items.prompt: Why do most turtles lay their eggs on land, even if they live in water?

options.label: Because their eggs need air and would drown in water
options.feedback: Correct. Turtle eggs have leathery shells and need to breathe air, so they must be laid in soil or sand on land, not under water.

options.label: Because the eggs need sunlight to hatch
options.feedback: Sunlight warms the sand, but the eggs do not need direct light to develop. They need air, and they are buried, not exposed to sun.

options.label: Because turtles cannot swim to lay eggs in water
options.feedback: Turtles are good swimmers, but eggs cannot survive submerged because they need oxygen. They come ashore specifically to lay eggs in air.

options.label: Because the water would wash the eggs away
options.feedback: That is a secondary reason, but the primary reason is that the eggs need to breathe. Even calm water would suffocate the embryo inside the egg.

items.ok_line: Turtle eggs must be laid on land to get oxygen.
items.ko_line: Air supply is the reason eggs go on land.
items.exp_text: Turtle eggs have a leathery shell that lets oxygen pass through. If laid underwater, the embryo would not get enough air and would die. So even marine turtles come ashore to bury their eggs in sand.

items.prompt: What happens to a turtle's body temperature when the surrounding air gets colder?

options.label: It stays the same because turtles are warm-blooded
options.feedback: Turtles are ectothermic, meaning they do not generate their own heat. Their body temperature changes with the environment.

options.label: It rises to keep them warm
options.feedback: Turtles cannot raise their own body temperature internally. They rely on outside heat sources like the sun.

options.label: It drops, because turtles are cold-blooded
options.feedback: Correct. Turtles are ectothermic, so their body temperature matches the temperature of their surroundings. When the air cools, so do they.

options.label: It only changes if they are in water, not on land
options.feedback: Whether on land or in water, a turtle's body temperature follows the environment. Cold air cools them just as cold water does.

items.ok_line: Turtles take on the temperature around them.
items.ko_line: Turtles cannot keep a constant body heat.
items.exp_text: Turtles are ectothermic, or cold-blooded. They do not produce their own body heat; instead, they warm up by basking in the sun and cool down when the air or water gets colder.
